turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Yeah, thank you for, um, fitting me in. So... I guess the main thing that finally pushed me to come in—and I've been thinking about doing this for a few months now, honestly, but I just kept putting it off—is that I’m having a really hard time at my job. 

I work as an insurance claims clerk, processing policies, which means I'm basically at a computer all day. And the issue is, I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, all the time. Even when I know, I absolutely know, I’m supposed to stay put and just finish my claim reviews. It's so frustrating because I'll sit down with a batch of claims, and I know I have a quota to hit, you know, they track how many we process and how fast we do them... but I'll get maybe halfway through reading one, and I just end up walking away from my desk. 

I'll go to the breakroom to check the coffee pot, or I'll walk down the hall for no real reason, or I'll just stand up and wander over to the printer even if I didn't print anything. And I know I shouldn't be doing it, I know I need to just stay in my chair and get the reviews done, but it's like I can't just stay seated. I just keep leaving my desk, and then I have to come back and figure out where I even was on the claim, and it's really starting to mess with my ability to actually get through my work.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they repeatedly leave their workstation and walk away from their desk when they are expected to stay seated and finish their work.

turns.doctor_question: When you do manage to stay seated at your desk, are you able to focus and concentrate on reading through the insurance claims, or does your mind feel like it's wandering and jumping around even when you're sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, that's... that's exactly it, actually. Even when I do manage to force myself to just stay in the chair, my brain is just absolutely all over the place. 

We have this open-plan office setup, which honestly I think was a terrible idea for a claims department because the cubicle walls are so low you can hear literally everything. So if I'm sitting there, trying my absolute hardest to just stare at my screen and read through a bodily injury claim or whatever, and the people in the next pod over start talking about a completely different claim—like maybe they're trying to figure out a coverage limit or complaining about a specific client—my brain just completely latches onto their conversation. I can't tune it out. 

And it doesn't even have to be the office noise, honestly. Sometimes it's just my own head. I'll be right in the middle of a complex paragraph about property damage, and suddenly I'll remember that I need to pick up paper towels on the way home, or I'll wonder if I paid my electric bill, or I'll just start thinking about some random errand I have to run on the weekend. 

When that happens, it's like my attention just completely slides right off what I’m reading. My eyes are still moving over the words, you know? Like, I'm physically still looking at the document and scrolling. But nothing is actually going in. I'll get to the bottom of the page and realize I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. So then I have to go back and reread the exact same section. And sometimes I have to reread it two, three, four times before the information actually sticks in my head, which just eats up so much time. It's so exhausting because it takes so much energy just to force my eyes to stay on the screen, and even then, if Brenda two desks down starts talking about her lunch, I'm suddenly fully invested in Brenda's lunch instead of the policy in front of me, and I have to start the whole rereading process all over again.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on reading tasks, noting their attention slides off and they have to reread sections multiple times.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they are easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (coworkers talking) and unrelated thoughts (remembering random errands).

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start noticing these difficulties with staying focused and sitting still? Was this something you struggled with back in school, or is this more of a recent problem that's developed over the past year or so?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because for a long time I really thought this was just a "now" problem, like maybe the open office or the boring claims were just finally getting to me. But when I really sit down and think about it... honestly, looking back, this definitely isn't brand new for me at all. Not even a little bit. 

I actually started thinking about this the other day, and I remembered how things were back when I was a kid. Like, way back in elementary school. I always felt like I was doing okay, you know, I wasn't failing or anything, but my parents kept all my old report cards in this big plastic bin in the basement, and I was looking through them a while ago. And it's crazy because every single year, it was the exact same story from every teacher. They would always write these little notes at the bottom, like, "He's a very bright boy, very capable," but then the next sentence was always, always about how I was losing my worksheets. I mean, I would just shove papers into my desk or my backpack and they would just disappear into the void. 

And they also wrote about how I would constantly miss instructions. Like, the teacher would stand at the front of the room and explain exactly how to do the math assignment, and I would be looking right at her, but my brain was just... somewhere else entirely, probably thinking about recess or a cartoon or something. And then everyone would start working, and I'd just be sitting there completely lost, having to ask the kid next to me what we were supposed to be doing. 

The teachers were always saying I needed constant reminders to actually finish my classwork, too. Because I'd start a worksheet, get maybe three problems in, and then I'd just start drawing in the margins or staring out the window, and the teacher would have to come tap on my desk and tell me to get back to work. So yeah, I guess when I really look at the whole picture, it's not just a recent thing at all. It's like I've always been this way, just kind of drifting off and losing track of things, even when I was just a little kid trying to get through third grade. It's just that now, instead of losing a spelling worksheet, I'm losing my place in a legal document, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks, noting they would start a worksheet, do a few problems, and then stare out the window.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient reports looking directly at the teacher while she spoke, but not actually listening because their mind was elsewhere.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions missing instructions and failing to finish classwork without constant reminders.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly recalls constantly losing worksheets and papers by shoving them into their desk or backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as thinking about recess or cartoons during class.

turns.doctor_question: Besides the difficulty staying in your chair at work, have you noticed that you tend to be restless or fidgety in other situations too—like when you're watching TV at home, or sitting through a meeting, or even just trying to relax? Do your hands or legs tend to move around a lot?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It's... it's not just that I get up, it's that even when I am technically stuck in a chair, I'm never actually still. 

Like, we have these mandatory team meetings every Tuesday morning, and then sometimes they make us do these really long quarterly compliance trainings, right? They book out the big conference room on the second floor for those. And I go in there, and I always tell myself, "Okay, just sit still, look professional, pretend you are locked in." Because I want to look focused, I really do. But man, within maybe five or ten minutes, my right leg is just going a mile a minute. I'll be bouncing my knee up and down under the table, completely unconsciously. Half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it until my knee bumps the underside of the table or I notice the water in somebody's glass vibrating a little bit. 

And then, you know, I'll catch myself and force my leg to stop. I'll press my foot flat on the floor and tell myself to just freeze. But the second I do that, the restlessness just moves somewhere else. I'll start shifting around in my chair endlessly. Those conference room chairs are those weird ergonomic mesh ones, and I just can't seem to find a position that feels right for more than two minutes. I'll cross my legs, then uncross them, lean to the left, sit back, lean forward on my elbows... I'm just constantly readjusting my weight. 

And the pens! If I have a pen in my hand—which I usually do, because we're supposed to be taking notes, even though they literally always just email us the PowerPoint deck afterwards anyway—I am just ruthlessly clicking it. Click, click, click, click. I actually had my supervisor, Dave, shoot me this really intense look across the table a couple of weeks ago because I was clicking my retractable pen over and over during a whole presentation on new underwriting guidelines. I felt terrible because I wasn't trying to be disruptive, my hands just needed something to do. 

So yeah, even when I'm trying my absolute hardest to just look like a normal, attentive person in a meeting or a training, I'm bouncing, clicking, shifting... it's like the energy just has to leak out of me somehow. And it's the same at home, honestly. If I'm on the couch trying to watch a movie, I'm usually flipping my phone over and over in my hand or shaking my foot the entire time. I just can't seem to turn the motor off.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes bouncing their knee, shifting endlessly in their chair, clicking a pen, and shaking their foot.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly notes feeling a sense of restlessness that 'just moves somewhere else' when they try to force themselves to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes feeling like energy has to leak out of them and states they 'just can't seem to turn the motor off', matching the 'driven by a motor' description.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to your childhood—say, before you turned 12 years old—do you remember having these same kinds of problems with sitting still and paying attention, or did those issues really only start showing up once you were older?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, like I was just mentioning a minute ago when we were talking about those old report cards, it really wasn't a brand new thing for me at all. I mean, thinking specifically about before I was 12—so, you know, early elementary school—it was exactly that same stuff I was just talking about. 

Like I said, the teachers would always start off the report cards nice, writing that I was a "bright boy" or that I was "very capable," but then it was just this laundry list of the exact same issues every single year. The losing worksheets thing was huge. I don't even know how I managed it, honestly, but my desk was just a complete black hole. I'd shove a paper in there and it would just get crushed under a million other things, just completely disappear. My mom used to get so frustrated because at parent-teacher conferences they'd always make me clean it out, and we'd find all these crumpled up, half-finished assignments from three weeks ago just stuffed in the back. 

And the missing instructions... yeah, that was definitely happening way back then, too. Like I was saying earlier, the teacher would be at the front of the room explaining a project or a math lesson, and I would be staring right at her, but my brain was just completely tuned out. I'd be watching a bug on the window or just daydreaming about whatever, and then suddenly the room gets loud and everyone is moving and opening their textbooks, and I'm just sitting there in a total panic because I have absolutely no idea what we're supposed to be doing or what page we're on. 

And then, of course, like I mentioned, they always had to give me constant reminders to actually finish my classwork. Because even if I did manage to figure out what to do, I'd do maybe one or two problems and then just start doodling in the margins or peeling the paper off my crayons. I had this one teacher in fourth grade, Mrs. Gable, who used to literally just walk by and tap on my desk with her knuckle every ten minutes. She wouldn't even say anything, just *tap tap*, because she knew if she didn't constantly pull my attention back to the paper, I would literally just stare at the wall until recess. So, yeah, it definitely goes way back before I was 12. It's pretty much always been there.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on classwork, doing only one or two problems before doodling or staring at the wall.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient notes that they would stare right at the teacher while she was explaining, but their brain would be completely tuned out.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions leaving assignments half-finished and needing constant reminders from teachers to actually finish their classwork.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their desk as a 'black hole' where papers were shoved and crushed under a million other things, indicating severe disorganization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states that losing worksheets was a huge issue and they would frequently lose papers in their messy desk.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as watching a bug on the window or daydreaming during lessons.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back to those early school years—before you were 12—do you remember your parents or teachers ever expressing concern that these attention and restlessness issues were actually causing you problems with your grades, or getting into trouble, or keeping up with your schoolwork?
turns.patient_response:
Well, back then... I mean, they were definitely annoyed, and there were always those parent-teacher conferences where my mom would come home looking super stressed out because of the missing assignments and the messy desk. But the thing was, I wasn't really failing. I was smart enough that I could usually cram at the last second or guess my way through a test, so my grades were mostly okay—like, mostly Bs and Cs. So my parents and teachers were concerned about my potential, you know, always saying I wasn't "living up to it" or that I was being lazy, but it wasn't completely ruining my life back then. I wasn't getting suspended or held back or anything like that. I always just managed to scrape by.

But honestly, the reason I've been thinking about all this so much lately—and why I'm even sitting here talking to you today—is because of how much it's actually impacting my life *now*. Like, scraping by in fourth grade is one thing, but work... work is a totally different story, and it's completely falling apart on me. 

Remember how I mentioned my supervisor, Dave? The one who gave me the dirty look for clicking my pen? Well, it's gone way past just him being annoyed with me in meetings. He actually pulled me into his office last week for a formal one-on-one, and... well, he put me on an official performance coaching plan. Which is basically just HR corporate-speak for "get it together right now or you're in major trouble." 

And it's all because my claim files are just completely falling behind. I have this huge queue of claims I'm supposed to be processing, and I just stare at the screen and can't make myself get through them fast enough, or I get distracted and lose my place and have to start reading the same file all over again. And worse than just being slow, Dave said my accuracy is being seriously questioned right now. I guess I've been missing key details in the policy documents, or putting the wrong codes into the system because my brain is just jumping all over the place and I'm rushing to catch up. 

And this is just... it's a total disaster for me, honestly. I've been at this company a while and I was really, really aiming for the senior adjuster track this year. It's a huge bump in pay, it's a better schedule, and I really wanted it. I thought I was next in line for it. But now, with this performance coaching thing on my record and my accuracy in the toilet, I am just terrified I'm going to lose that opportunity entirely. It just feels like my brain is literally costing me my career at this point, and I just... I can't seem to stop it from happening, no matter how hard I try to focus.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports making careless mistakes at work, such as missing key details in policy documents and entering incorrect codes.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes difficulty sustaining attention on work tasks, noting they lose their place and have to reread the same files.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions failing to finish schoolwork ('missing assignments') in childhood and currently failing to complete workplace duties ('claim files are just completely falling behind').
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient recalls having a 'messy desk' during childhood, indicating difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they get distracted while trying to process their claim files.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient references a previous mention of clicking their pen, which is a form of fidgeting.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in elementary school, did these attention and restlessness problems actually hold you back in any real way—like, did you fall behind your classmates academically, have trouble making friends, or get into trouble at school because of them? Or was it more just that your teachers were frustrated but you were still keeping up okay overall?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, so, kind of like I was just saying a second ago, it was definitely more the second thing. I wasn't falling behind academically in any kind of permanent way. I mean, I never had to repeat a grade or go to summer school or anything drastic like that. 

Like I mentioned, I was getting mostly Bs and Cs because I could figure things out at the last possible second. I was basically the king of the panic-cram. Like, if we had a spelling test or a vocabulary quiz on a Friday, I wouldn't even look at the words Monday through Thursday. I'd lose the list, or forget it in my desk, and then Thursday night my mom would find out and be drilling me at the kitchen table while I was just completely overwhelmed and frustrated, but I'd still manage to pull off a B-minus or a C-plus the next morning. So on paper, I looked fine. I kept up okay, even if the process of getting there was a total mess behind the scenes. 

And as far as getting into trouble... I wasn't a bad kid at all. I wasn't getting sent to the principal's office for fighting or being defiant or anything. It was really just... exasperation. The teachers were just constantly exasperated with me. Like Mrs. Gable with her tapping on my desk. She wasn't furious with me, she was just tired of me staring at the window instead of my math sheet. And making friends was never really an issue either. I was pretty sociable—maybe a little too talkative when I was actually supposed to be reading quietly, which probably annoyed the teachers even more—but the other kids liked me fine. 

So yeah, it didn't really hold me back back then. It was just a lot of friction, I guess you could call it. A lot of friction and annoyed adults, but no real, life-altering consequences. Not like now with Dave and the HR stuff. That's why it's all so jarring to me lately, because back then I could just skate by on being a "bright boy" who just needed to apply himself, but you can't really pull that off when you're 26 and messing up actual insurance claims, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions losing their spelling list or forgetting it in their desk.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient recalls staring out the window instead of focusing on their math sheet.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient admits to being 'a little too talkative' when they were supposed to be reading quietly.
symptom_reasoning.S075: The patient denies having trouble making friends, stating they were sociable and liked by other kids.
symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient explicitly denies getting into fights or being defiant at school.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to those elementary school years, do you remember your parents or teachers ever saying that these attention and restlessness problems were actually causing real problems for you—like, was it affecting your ability to do things you wanted to do, or causing you problems at home or with other kids, or keeping you from activities you cared about?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, it really is just like I was saying a minute ago. I mean, I don't think they ever felt like it was ruining my life or anything like that. Because, you know, when it came to things I actually *wanted* to do? I was totally fine. Like, it never kept me from my activities or anything. If anything, my mom would get more annoyed because she’d see me out in the yard building this incredibly elaborate fort out of cardboard boxes for three hours straight, completely focused, or I'd be playing video games until dinner, and then she’d be like, "Why can't you just do that with your spelling worksheet?" So it definitely wasn't stopping me from having fun or doing the stuff I cared about. 

And at home... I mean, yeah, like I said, my mom was stressed about the messy desk and those Thursday night cram sessions, but it wasn't causing, like, massive family blowouts. I wasn't getting grounded for weeks on end or anything. It was just this constant, low-level annoyance for her. She'd sigh a lot, you know? Like, "Here we go again with the missing paper." But we still had a totally normal family life otherwise. We went on camping trips, we watched movies together. It wasn't this dark cloud hanging over the whole house. My dad worked a lot, so he wasn't as involved in the day-to-day homework battles, but even he just kind of saw it as me being a bit scatterbrained. 

And with other kids, like I mentioned, I was always pretty social. I had my group of friends, we rode bikes around the neighborhood, traded cards, all that normal kid stuff. None of them cared if I lost my math homework or if Mrs. Gable had to tap on my desk. Kids don't really pay attention to that stuff unless you're, like, throwing chairs or something, which I never did. 

So, no, I really don't remember anyone saying it was causing *real* damage to my life back then. It was just... I was just the disorganized kid who daydreamed too much. That was my label. It's just so crazy to think about how different it is now, because back then the worst thing that happened was my mom giving me a lecture at the kitchen table, and now I'm literally sitting in HR meetings sweating through my shirt because Dave is looking at my claim processing times and telling me I'm missing policy details. It's just... it's a completely different world now. When you're a kid, people just kind of cover for you or push you along, but nobody is doing that for me at the insurance firm.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient recalls childhood incidents of the 'missing paper' and having 'lost my math homework'.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that they were known as the kid who 'daydreamed too much'.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned that back in elementary school, you were mostly getting Bs and Cs and keeping up okay overall. But I want to ask you more specifically: did these attention and restlessness problems ever cause you to actually miss out on things that mattered to you, or cause real problems between you and your parents or teachers—not just frustration, but actual conflict or consequences that stuck with you?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, no. I know it probably sounds like I’m just repeating myself, or maybe like I’m downplaying it, but I promise I’m really not. It just truly never got to that level of actual, serious conflict. 

As far as missing out on things... no, never. My parents weren't really the strict, authoritarian types, you know? They wouldn't ground me from hanging out with my friends or take away my weekends just because my desk was a disaster area or I forgot my vocabulary words. I mean, maybe once in a blue moon I had to stay inside for an extra fifteen minutes during recess to finish a worksheet I was supposed to do during class, but that was really the absolute worst of it. It never kept me from doing the things I actually cared about. 

And with my parents and teachers, it was never an adversarial thing. There were no screaming matches at the dinner table. My mom never yelled, she just... she'd just sit at the kitchen table rubbing her temples, looking completely drained. And my teachers, like Mrs. Gable or my fifth-grade teacher, they never yelled either. They just looked at me with this sort of mix of pity and total exhaustion. 

So there really weren't any lasting consequences back then. It's not like I have this deep childhood trauma of being severely punished for not paying attention. The consequences were entirely... I don't know, invisible, I guess? It was mostly just me feeling kind of stupid sometimes when I'd suddenly realize everyone else in the room knew exactly what page we were on and I was still staring out the window at the parking lot. But no one was screaming at me, and it didn't ruin my relationships.

And I think... I think that's exactly why this whole situation with Dave at work is hitting me like a ton of bricks right now. I don't have any experience with actual, real-world consequences for this stuff. When you're nine years old, people just give you a pass. They sigh, they tap your desk, they help you find your missing paper, and life goes on. But when you're twenty-six and you're processing insurance claims that affect people's actual money and the company's bottom line... there are no passes. Dave isn't going to just sigh and help me find my place in the policy document. He's going to fire me. And that's just terrifying, because I feel like I'm trying just as hard to focus now as I was back then, but the safety net is completely gone and I'm just in freefall.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient mentions trying hard to focus both now and in the past, indicating an ongoing struggle with sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their childhood desk as a 'disaster area', highlighting difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient recalls teachers having to help them find their 'missing paper', indicating a tendency to lose necessary items.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes losing their place in class because they were 'staring out the window at the parking lot', demonstrating distractibility by extraneous stimuli.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to elementary school, do you remember your parents or teachers ever saying that your attention or restlessness problems were actually making it hard for you to do your schoolwork, or that they were concerned enough about it to want you to see a doctor or get some kind of help?
turns.patient_response:
I feel like a broken record here, but honestly, no. It really never crossed that line for anyone. 

Like I was saying about the Thursday night cramming, they definitely knew the homework was a battle, but they never said it was making it impossible for me to *do* the work, if that makes sense. Because I *could* do it, eventually. My mom would always use that exact phrase—"He has the brains, he just doesn't apply himself." That was the big takeaway. I just needed to apply myself more. 

And as for seeing a doctor or getting some kind of professional help? No way. That never even came up. Not once. I don't know if it was just the school I was at or how things were back then, but nobody was jumping to send a kid to a doctor just because his desk looked like a paper recycling bin had exploded inside it. They just viewed it as a discipline thing, or an organizational issue. 

My mom's solution was never a doctor. Her solution was Office Depot. Every single August, right before school started, we'd go and buy these incredibly elaborate planner systems. She'd get me those big Trapper Keepers with the different colored folders—like, red was always for math, blue for science, green for language arts. And she'd buy these special daily assignment notebooks where I was supposed to write down every single thing the teacher wrote on the chalkboard. She really thought that if I just had the right binder, I'd magically become this perfectly organized, focused student. 

And, I mean, of course, by the second week of October, the folders were ripped, half my worksheets were just shoved loose into the bottom of my backpack, and the planner was completely lost. But her reaction to that was never, "Oh, maybe there's an underlying issue here, let's call the pediatrician." It was just, "Why aren't you using the system we bought? Why are you being so careless?" 

So, yeah, nobody ever suggested getting me actual help. It was just assumed I'd grow out of it, or that I'd figure it out eventually if I just tried harder. Which I guess I sort of faked my way through enough to get through high school and some of college, just by the skin of my teeth. But now... yeah. Now it's just me and Dave and a mountain of mismatched insurance claims, and no color-coded folder is going to save my job. I actually went to the store and bought a planner a few weeks ago, thinking maybe it would help me track my processing times for HR, but I haven't even opened it. It's just sitting on my desk right now. So, no, to answer your question, nobody ever thought it was a medical thing back then.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes a history of severe disorganization, noting his childhood desk looked like an exploded recycling bin and his worksheets were shoved loosely into his backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states that his school planner was 'completely lost' shortly after the school year started.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at elementary school, when you think about all these attention and restlessness problems—the daydreaming, losing papers, needing constant reminders—do you remember that actually getting in the way of your grades or your ability to keep up with what the other kids were doing academically, even if you eventually managed to pass?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... no, not really. Like I mentioned before, I was mostly getting Bs and Cs, so I wasn't failing anything. It really didn't get in the way of my actual grades or stop me from moving up to the next grade level with all my friends. I was never in remedial classes or anything like that. Because, the thing is, elementary school academics just aren't that... demanding, I guess? 

Like, I could be completely zoned out while Mrs. Gable was explaining long division on the overhead projector, just staring at the dust motes floating in the light, completely in my own world. But then she'd hand out the worksheet, and I could usually just look at the example problem at the top of the page and kind of reverse-engineer it in my head well enough to get, you know, seven out of ten right. And that was a passing grade. So I kept up just fine. 

Same with spelling tests or vocabulary—I would literally just memorize the list on the bus ride to school on Friday morning. I'd just stare at the words for twenty minutes, take the test, get a B, and then immediately forget all of them by lunchtime. So on paper, if you just looked at my report cards, I looked like a totally average, middle-of-the-pack student. The teacher's comments in the margins would always say stuff like, "A pleasure to have in class, but easily distracted," or "Needs to pay better attention during quiet reading time," but the actual letter grades were completely fine. It never actually stopped me from keeping up with what everyone else was doing. 

And I think that's why nobody caught on that I was struggling to pay attention, because the results were so... normal. I was smart enough to just sort of float by without really locking in. But that's the thing, right? You can't just float by when you're dealing with complex commercial liability policies. You can't just look at an example claim and reverse-engineer it in five minutes, because every single policy has different exclusions and riders, and if you miss one detail because you zoned out, you're costing the company thousands of dollars. And Dave knows that. So yeah, back then, no, it didn't hurt my grades at all. The daydreaming didn't cost me anything academically. But now it's costing me everything, and I just don't know how to fix it since I've literally never had to before.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes missing details at work because of zoning out, which costs the company money and is currently 'costing me everything'.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in elementary school, thinking about all these attention and restlessness problems together—the daydreaming, losing papers, needing reminders—did they actually cause you real problems that you or your parents noticed as being significant, like struggling to keep up with schoolwork despite trying, having trouble with friendships, or causing real tension at home? Or was it really just that your teachers found it frustrating but everything basically worked out okay for you?
turns.patient_response:
I know I probably sound like I’m just giving you the exact same answer again, but it really, truly was just that second thing you said. It was frustrating for the teachers, sure, but everything basically worked out totally fine for me. 

I didn't have any trouble with friendships at all, actually. Like, I was always right in the middle of whatever we were doing at recess. We'd play wall-ball or trade Pokémon cards by the chain-link fence, and, I mean, none of those kids cared if I forgot my spelling words or if my backpack was just a black hole of crumpled-up worksheets. Kids don't care about that stuff, you know? They just care if you're fun to play with. So socially, I was completely fine. I never felt left out or alienated or anything like that.

And at home... I mean, I told you about the whole elaborate planner system my mom would try to set up every year, so she was definitely annoyed sometimes. But it wasn't like... real tension, if that makes sense? It wasn't this dark, heavy cloud hanging over our house. We'd still have family movie nights, we'd go get pizza on Fridays, and she wasn't constantly riding me about my focus. It was just an occasional, "Oh, there he goes again, losing his homework" kind of annoyance. 

So it really just fell on the teachers to deal with it. And honestly, bless them, because I'm sure I was exhausting to have in class. I can literally still picture Mrs. Gable just closing her eyes and taking this slow, deep breath when she'd walk by and see me, like, drawing on the rubber part of my shoe instead of doing the silent reading assignment. But they just dealt with it. They'd tap my desk, point to the paragraph I was supposed to be on, and that was it. I'd get my C-plus and move on with my life. It never ruined anything for me back then. 

Which is just... I don't know, it's honestly so frustrating to think about now. Because part of me wishes someone *had* made it a real problem back then. If it had been a huge deal when I was ten, maybe we would have figured something out, and maybe I wouldn't be sitting here at twenty-six, completely terrified that Dave is going to pull me into his office and fire me over these backed-up insurance claims. Because back then, the absolute highest stakes were just a heavy sigh from a teacher, and now the stakes are my rent and my entire livelihood, and I just... I don't have the tools for it. But yeah, to answer your question, it wasn't a real problem back then. I just sort of floated through.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes drawing on their shoe instead of doing a silent reading assignment in school, indicating difficulty sustaining attention on tasks.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned getting mostly Bs and Cs in elementary school, but I want to understand this better: compared to your classmates, were you actually keeping up academically at the same level they were, or were you falling behind and just managing to pass because you were smart enough to catch up at the last minute?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... I guess it’s kind of hard to say exactly where I was compared to everyone else, because I wasn't really paying attention to what they were doing either. But... if I had to really think about it, I’d say I was keeping up just fine. It wasn't like I was drowning and then suddenly pulling off a miracle at the end of the semester. It was more like... I was just sort of bobbing along with the current, you know? 

Like, I remember in fourth grade, we had this big unit on the Oregon Trail. Everyone was obsessed with it because we got to play the computer game during free time. And the actual assignment was to keep this journal from the perspective of a pioneer. Some kids, like this girl Sarah who sat next to me, she had this incredibly detailed journal with drawings of the wagon and lists of provisions and she even burned the edges of the paper to make it look old. She was definitely operating on a different level. But then there were kids who just wrote, "Today we crossed a river. An ox died." And I was somewhere right in the middle. I’d write enough to show I understood the assignment, maybe throw in a detail about dysentery because it was funny, and that was it. I got a B. I wasn't falling behind the kid who wrote about the dead ox, but I definitely wasn't doing what Sarah was doing. 

So, I don't think I was falling behind. I was just doing exactly what was required to stay in the middle of the pack. I didn't feel like I was constantly playing catch-up, mostly because I just didn't care enough to try and be at the top. It was just... I’d do the bare minimum, get my C-plus or B-minus, and then go out to recess. And it worked. It worked perfectly fine for years. Until it didn't. Because now, with these claims, Dave isn't grading on a curve. He expects Sarah-level attention to detail on every single file, and I’m still just writing about the dead ox, you know? And I can't figure out how to bridge that gap. So, yeah, back then, I was definitely keeping up with the average kid, just not... excelling, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly states they are currently unable to provide the required 'attention to detail on every single file' at work, comparing their current work to doing the bare minimum.

turns.doctor_question: When you look back at your elementary school years, do you think you were actually performing at the level you were capable of academically, or do you think you were underperforming compared to what you could have done if you had been able to focus better?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... honestly? If I really think about it, I definitely wasn't performing at the level I was capable of. I was totally underperforming, even if it didn't look like it on paper because I was getting those Bs and Cs. Because, like I said, I was bright enough to just sort of coast. 

But looking back at it now, with everything going on at work with Dave and the insurance policies... it's like this giant lightbulb just went off, you know? Because this feeling of just barely skating by, of not living up to my potential... this wasn't brand new for me. It really wasn't. Like, I remember—and this is so clear now that I'm actually thinking about it—I remember my mom keeping all my report cards in this big accordion folder in the bottom drawer of the filing cabinet in the den. And every single year, from like second grade all the way through fifth, the teachers would write the exact same kind of comments in that little box at the bottom. 

It was always some variation of, "He is a very bright boy, but..." And then the "but" was always this laundry list of things that are literally exactly what I'm doing now at work. They'd write that I was bright, but I constantly lost my worksheets. Or that I was smart, but I always missed the verbal instructions when she was standing right at the front of the room talking to us. Or they'd say I needed constant reminders just to finish basic classwork that everyone else was already done with. 

Like, I remember Mrs. Gable—I keep bringing her up, but she was my fourth-grade teacher and she was so strict—she actually wrote in red pen once, "He has so much potential if he could just apply himself and keep track of his assignments." And my mom was so annoyed, she made me sit at the kitchen table and reorganize my entire Trapper Keeper, which took like three hours because I had shoved so many loose, half-finished math sheets into the pockets that they were all ripped and crinkled. 

So, yeah. I was smart enough to pass, and I guess that's why no one sounded the alarm. But I definitely wasn't doing what I could have been doing if I had just been able to focus and keep track of my stuff like a normal kid. And it's just wild to me that I'm sitting here at twenty-six, and my boss is essentially telling me the exact same thing Mrs. Gable told my mom when I was ten. It's like I've been stuck in this same loop my entire life, just losing papers and missing instructions, and I never even realized it until my job was on the line.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient recalls missing verbal instructions even when the teacher was speaking directly to the class.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions needing constant reminders to finish basic classwork and having half-finished math sheets.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes having a disorganized Trapper Keeper filled with loose, crinkled papers that took hours to reorganize.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they constantly lost their worksheets and papers during elementary school.
